chapter_theme: Understanding and goodness are not sealed within a person; they take on the nature of the company one keeps, as water takes on its soil. The chapter gradually grants the mind its goodness while insisting that company still strengthens or spoils it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as an argument: the small company doesn't suit the great (451), why, through the soil image (452), replies to those who locate everything in the mind (453-454), how understanding comes through company (455), and the merit of good company, to those who think it unneeded (456-459), ending with the positive and negative stated together (460).

451.reading: Greatness fears the small company; smallness at once takes it as kin.
451.nuance: The verse gives the fear to greatness, not to a person lacking resolve. Parimelazhagar explains it through self-knowledge: the wise know their judgment can bend, while the small see only likeness and suspect nothing.

452.reading: As water changes by the nature of the land, so a person's understanding becomes the nature of their company.
452.nuance: Note the subject: it is அறிவு that changes, not behaviour or reputation. Parimelazhagar sharpens the image, with water pure in the sky and only turning on contact, and so with understanding held alone.

453.reading: A person's perception comes from the mind; the word 'such a one' comes from their company.
453.nuance: A clean division of labour: faculty is inner and reputation is social. Parimelazhagar assigns the mind only basic sense-awareness and gives all cultivated judgment to company, a step further than the verse says. Manakkudavar makes the word specifically blame.

454.reading: Understanding, while showing itself as though in the mind, lies for a person in their company.
454.nuance: The verse is one of the Kural's most radical on the self: where understanding appears to be is not where it is. Parimelazhagar's 'the mind is where it shows, the company is its root' makes it explicit. The verse doesn't explain why.

455.reading: Purity of mind and purity of deeds, these two, come leaning on purity of company.
455.nuance: தூவா is a rare word, which Parimelazhagar glosses as a support and defends with a citation. The claim is causal: company is the thing the other two rest on, not a third kind of purity alongside them.

456.reading: Those pure of mind have a good எச்சம்; for those pure of company there is no deed that doesn't turn out well.

positions.position: எச்சம் is children: effects don't differ from their causes.
எச்சம் is the wealth that remains after one.
positions.quote: மனநல்லார்க்குப் பின்பு நிற்கும் காண முதலான பொருள்கள் நல்லவாம்;

457.reading: Goodness of mind gains a person prosperity; goodness of company gives all praise as well.
457.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason for the second clause is neat: those able to give praise are the good themselves, and they are the company.

458.reading: Though the worthy have goodness of mind in full, goodness of company is a protection to them.
458.nuance: The verse makes its concession to the mind here, then refuses to let it stand alone. Even சான்றோர் are not exempt.

positions.position: Good company keeps nurturing a goodness of mind that came from earlier good deeds.
positions.quote: அந் நல்வினை உள்வழியும் மனநலத்தை வளர்த்து வருதலின்

positions.position: The protection is social: good company keeps the worthy from being looked down on.

459.reading: From goodness of mind comes the next world, and even that gains strength from goodness of company.
459.nuance: The verse names மறுமை in plain terms in the book on polity. Parimelazhagar notes that goodness of mind can slip from time to time, and good company holds it steady.

positions.position: The verse concerns joy in the next life, which the mind's goodness yields and good company secures.
He doesn't mention the next life. The verse is about the support that company gives to a firm mind.

460.reading: There is no greater support than good company and nothing that brings more affliction than bad company.
460.nuance: Parimelazhagar says the chapter's title, avoiding small company, has been argued mainly from the reverse: by praising good company. Only this last verse states both sides together.

links.note: 373 says a person's own understanding prevails over all study; 454 says understanding only seems to be one's own and lies in one's company. These are two different accounts of where knowledge comes from, within or among others, and they don't fit together easily.
34 makes a spotless mind the whole of virtue. 455 makes that purity lean on purity of company. If so, the root of virtue in 34 has a root of its own outside the person.
114 says worthiness is seen by one's எச்சம், and 456 says purity of mind produces a good one. The same disputed word closes the loop between what is inward and what is left behind.

428 says the knowing fear what should be feared. 451 names one such object, a surprising one: not a danger, but a social circle. It only makes sense given 452's claim that company changes understanding.

source_issues: 459: Kalaignar's commentary reads much like his comment on 458 and doesn't address மறுமை. It appears to be about the right verse but may be thin rather than a deliberate position, so the contest here is weaker than it looks.
